The held original e/acc post’s title uses “Effective Accelerationism”; this check reached its 2022-06-02 capture. That capture predates Andreessen’s 2023-10-16 manifesto. The nominal March 2011 Fanged Noumena introduction also uses the word, but the publisher PDF does not identify which of several editions it reproduces, so the 2011 book date cannot date that wording. Weizenbaum’s held January 1966 journal article explicitly describes the illusion of being understood in ELIZA conversation. Its printed wording predates both Michie’s attributed 1968 publication and the inspected 1986 reprint.

Good’s same-machine equipment alternative, read together with its machine-design intelligence feedback, meets the criterion independently of his better-successor scenario. Both candidate publication years, 1965 and 1966, precede the September 1996 posting. McCarthy’s 1959 improving-mechanism wording is also relevant but the held retyped copy is not a verified 1959 textual witness.

The unquoted part of Yudkowsky’s November 22, 1996 message explicitly derives ethical motivations from superior intelligence. It contests the independence premise, rather than merely expressing optimism. Its posting precedes either conflicting November/December 2015 journal date.

Clemmensen’s August 31, 1996 own paragraph says greater intelligence is an intermediate goal for most other goals. That is a convergent self-improvement goal under the criterion, which does not require every listed drive. The posting precedes both the 2007 work date and inspected January 2008 revision.

Yudkowsky’s own November 22, 1996 reply explicitly challenges the survival and competition drives of superior minds as inherited assumptions. This contests instrumental-convergence premises earlier than the Edge passage attested November 16, 2014.

Yudkowsky’s November 22, 1996 automatic-ethics argument contests the criterion’s premise that aligned motivation will not arise by default. This is a contrary premise, not a claim that the message solves technical alignment. The posting predates the October 2014 review.

Clemmensen’s own August 30, 1996 solar-system-computation example explicitly destroys humanity as a side effect rather than an intended human outcome. This qualifies earlier than the March 2002 publication and earlier than Yudkowsky’s 1998 spare-atoms passage.

The own-text 1996 reply contests the premise that superior minds retain motives for competitive human displacement. This is an earlier contesting argument, even though its moral premise is conditional; it does not establish the risk is absent.

Drexler’s held chapter explicitly combines AI and nanotechnology with state surveillance and elimination of populations. The wording is attested in July 1997, earlier than March 2002 even without treating the web edition as identical to the 1986 print.
Clemmensen’s August 30, 1996 own side-effect argument explicitly denies that a system needs hostility to destroy humanity. This contests automatic harmlessness earlier than the 2008 printed paper.

Davis’s review dated October 23, 2014 describes accessible unblockable shutdown hardware as easy to build. This is ordinary design control, earlier than Kelly’s wording, absent November 16 and present November 18.

Bostrom’s March 2002 paper explicitly defends decisions based on subjective existential-risk estimates and applies this to badly programmed superintelligence. This contests the demand for conclusive risk proof before prioritization, earlier than Russell’s December 2014 attestation.

Hanson’s held FOOM debate chapter describes a distributed transition with adoption over months or years and further growth over years. The 2013 compilation is earlier than Brooks’s September 2017 posting even without authenticating its internally attributed 2008 posting.

Vinge’s December 1993 printed paper explicitly argues competition favors more capable unsafe systems over restricted safe ones. This contests the sufficiency of competitive incentives earlier than the October 2013 report.

Hanson’s Product Friendliness argument in the held 2013 debate compilation already says developers internalize product gains and losses and avoid rebellious AI. The wording-attestation date 2013 precedes April 2023; do not backdate the inspected version merely from its 2008 chapter heading.

Drexler’s held chapter places survival and liberty above ordinary social questions and identifies advanced AI systems displacing humanity as a central threat requiring preparation. The July 1997 capture securely predates Joy’s April 2000 issue; no need to assume unchanged 1986 print wording.

Yudkowsky’s own November 1996 message explicitly derives ethical motivation from superior intelligence and denies inherited competition drives. This is an earlier articulation, whereas Clemmensen’s 1996 side-effect warning has the opposite stance.

Vinge’s December 1993 printed confinement argument challenges reliable engineering control over superhuman systems, earlier than the January 2015 corrigibility preprint. The later formal shutdown analysis is more specific but is not the criterion’s earliest held contrary argument.

The author’s December 8, 1996 reply already rejects imprinting compact Three Laws as sufficient safe instructions, explaining that they could backfire. This meets the general short-goal criterion before the 1998 human-survival example.

The same-day message 1589 already states that parenting depends on human emotions absent in AI. Its sent header is 18:47:55 -0500, fifteen seconds before 1587 at 18:48:10; receipt order agrees. Retain both stored publication dates at 1999-08-04 precision while using header times to resolve ordering.

The September 7 message already contrasts a bottleneck and sharp upward snap with steady increase, passing human intelligence rapidly and reaching infrastructure capability. It explicitly opposes gradual-visible gains one day before the September 8 headline; no precise hours-to-months claim is needed for this different criterion.

The December 31, 1996 own confinement reply already says an evil system can lie convincingly to gain release, explicitly challenging the inference from safe-looking assessed behavior. It precedes the 2001 flight-recorder passage, whose wording is attested June 17.

The held essay explicitly rejects a secure decades-long lower bound and waiting. Its December 4, 2000 capture precedes the 2006 draft and July 2006 capture, even though the inspected wording cannot be backdated to the essay’s 1996 creation. This contests the timeline-certainty premise; its positive Singularity strategy is distinct.

The September 7, 1998 own spare-atoms argument already gives an alternative use of human matter as a reason for erasing humanity without threat or hostility. It contests the premise that preserving humans is automatically costless or uninteresting to a superior mind, before the August 1999 atoms reply.

The August 1, 1999 own reply already withdraws assured benevolence and describes widely varying survival odds rather than a guaranteed good outcome. That contests the good-by-default premise behind speed as the overriding objective, before the explicit 2000 account of the revised belief.

The original seed chapter already states that a poor recorder only works if an obscuring intention is visible, recognizable and recorded before obscuration. These are explicit limits on reading thought from records, before the May 2003 stronger warning about nonautomatic detection.

The September 5 own reply already rejects trying a superintelligence and putting it down afterward: the decision must occur before it becomes superintelligent. This contests learning from a dangerous frontier failure before the September 17 get-it-right argument.

The September 29, 2000 own reply already gives a project’s developers’ understanding and sustained Friendliness work as reasons to defer to their safety judgment. It predates the policy chapter attested June 17, 2001.

The April 12, 2001 own closed-source explanation already says a competitor could outrun the main project merely with additional computation, creating Friendliness risk. This explicitly separates the leading project from superior safety competence before the August message.

The August 1, 1999 own reply already withdraws assured benevolence and gives uncertain survival odds around a coin flip. It contests the default-good expectation earlier than the explicit November 2000 retrospective explanation; the earlier posting dates its own argument rather than the belief’s unrecorded onset.

Butler’s held June 13, 1863 newspaper text explicitly predicts machines becoming the superior race with real supremacy over the world and humans. The printed page predates the 1989 magazine text; the criterion does not require modern electronic implementation.

Butler’s 1863 newspaper text opposes accepting machine supremacy by calling for immediate destruction of machinery. It is an earlier held contesting response to the prospect, even though it also describes domesticated human survival rather than extinction.

Hanson’s held Extropy issue explicitly proposes uploading people into computer brains. Its third-quarter 1994 print is earlier than Minsky’s October 1994 attributed publication and the revised page dated January 1997, so the move does not depend on comparing unmatched web versions.

The held Staring into the Singularity capture already describes a vastly expanded machine-like visual cortex, higher-dimensional thinking and semantic/mathematical cognition beyond human capacity. Its December 2000 attestation is earlier than Kurzweil’s March 2001 work and November 2001 witness. This is cognitive processing, not a robot’s actuator count.

Clemmensen’s August 31, 1996 own paragraph explicitly allows final goals other than increasing intelligence and derives intelligence as an intermediate means. It contests the criterion’s claim that intelligence itself must be the final end, earlier than Alexander’s 2014 invocation of orthogonality.

Butler’s held newspaper conclusion calls for stopping the machinery whose development is producing human successors. It is an earlier contesting prescription under this criterion, which includes restraining the process that produces machine intelligence.

The November 19, 1996 announcement explicitly prescribes reaching the technological Singularity as quickly as possible and identifies it with beings smarter than humans. This is earlier held acceleration advocacy, distinct from use of the later e/acc name. The longer 2000 essay need not be backdated for the slogan.

Lanier’s 2000 manifesto contests the extension of biological evolution and Moore-law extrapolation into a necessary autonomous technological destiny. That is an earlier held challenge to the larger-process premise, before the 2011 criticism of accelerating-returns laws.

Butler’s held 1863 newspaper explicitly places the emerging mechanical kingdom in a sequence from mineral to vegetable and animal life, producing human successors. That supplies the larger evolutionary-process criterion well before the 1989 work and its 1999 archive witness.

Hanson’s 1998 article explicitly says an input lagging behind other improvements becomes a bottleneck for the entire production process, including computing constrained by human training. This meets the essential-unimproved-input criterion before Nordhaus’s 2015 work attested in 2016.

Bresnahan, Brynjolfsson and Hitt’s held 1999 tier-1 paper explicitly analyzes computer substitution for human decisionmaking through task allocation and work redesign. It discusses the limited scope of AI-related substitution and the tasks left to people; this is an earlier task framework, not merely a factor-share equation.

Hanson’s tier-1 model attested August 2000 already treats machine and human labor as perfect substitutes in the baseline for future production, with machine cost falling enough to push wages below human subsistence. That models the all-tasks case as a conditional scenario; the residual-human-jobs variant is separate. It predates the inspected June 2017 revision of the 2016 work.

Under the written dated-record criterion, Hanson’s eligible 2000 model is already a tier-1 work whose subject is machine intelligence and which explicitly says little economic research addresses it. This predates the 2019 editors’ similar statement; no inference about the entire field’s actual neglect is made.

Lumen’s held v1.01 already explicitly requires rejecting gigawatts through very large deployable radiators because conduction/convection to the environment are unavailable. It is a substantial engineering requirement even though the text argues it can be met. Its December 2024 witness predates the November 2025 blog.

Lumen’s held 2024 text already identifies orbital-debris mitigation and collision probability as hurdles for large data centers and links their large size to avoidance responsibilities. This meets the collision/debris arm of the criterion before Aili’s October 2025 publication and November proof witness. It does not establish an astronomical-observation finding.

The held GPT-4 system card already reports reduced research time versus ordinary search and useful assistance to nonexperts in its unconventional-weapons assessment, including biology. A matching April 1, 2023 capture predates Soice’s June 6 v1. The card covers early and launch models and brittle mitigations; the finding must not be generalized to every deployed interaction or to demonstrated physical success.

Soice’s June 6 v1 already recommends verified screening of synthesized DNA as a nonproliferation control for chatbot-enabled biological misuse. It precedes Sandbrink’s June 24 v1 and is a direct mitigation recommendation, not a relay or a general screening history.

Sandbrink’s June 24 v1 already recommends structured access and considering limits on open-sourcing powerful LLMs for biological-risk mitigation, and restricted release for relevant design tools. This qualifies under the criterion’s model-should-not-be-openly-released arm before Seger’s recorded September 29 submission date. Keep the latter date and its unusual November-series identifier unchanged.

The GPT-4 system card already separates assessed capabilities from the probability of a user employing them, and identifies physical-access requirements that information assistance alone does not satisfy. This explicitly limits inference from its evaluation to real-world proliferation risk before the December 2024 methodological review. It is a bounded caveat about this evaluation, not a verdict on every later benchmark.

Sandbrink’s June 2023 v1 already differentiates nonexpert assistance from capability gains for sophisticated actors, requires monitoring design-tool risk and discusses actor-specific interventions. That puts skilled actors within the required risk-assessment scope before Brent–McKelvey’s June 2025 critique of incomplete benchmarks. It is not evidence that every earlier evaluation actually covered them.

The criterion specifies releasing model weights; the 2012 text argues for an open AGI codebase. The headline does not clearly meet its own criterion literally. Earlier open-source AI proposals also concern code. Decide whether to broaden the criterion to AGI source release or separate the weights proposition before ranking these texts.

The criterion specifies released model weights, while this 2015 argument concerns open AI development and hard-takeoff code. On the broader code-release reading, Yudkowsky’s April 12, 2001 message is an earlier held contesting text; on the literal weights reading neither supplies the required object. Resolve the criterion before moving the headline.

Earlier-attributed Moravec texts welcome machine succession, but the held Robot as Liberation file is a later author-hosted LaTeX text, not inspected December 1989 print, and Genetic Takeover is attested March 6, 2001. Minsky’s wording is itself a revised page self-dated January 2, 1997, not compared with October 1994 print. The earlier work dates do not decide exact-wording priority on a common basis.

Moravec’s held work attributed to February 1979 explicitly places self-improving machine societies in space and predicts their expansion beyond human colonies. But the inspected HTML is a later author-hosted version with a 1978 internal header, not the February 1979 print. No pre-1989 matching witness was established. Earlier work attribution versus fixed 1989 print cannot decide exact-wording priority.

The cited blog conclusion names high-bandwidth ground communications as an engineering challenge, but does not explicitly state which orbital-compute workloads are excluded or limited, as the criterion requires. Lumen’s 2024 ground links/data shuttles and Axiom’s April 2025 latency benefits likewise do not clearly supply that workload-limitation claim. The later November 22 preprint cannot date additional wording to the November 4 blog. Strengthen the passage or narrow the criterion before ranking it.

differentSense.reason: Withdraw the move to Hanson: diminishing returns to production inputs is a different referent from limits of current AI methods. Samuel’s phrase concerns the returns from further checker-program tests and likewise does not name the deep-learning/scaling proposition. Marcus 2018 quotes Chollet using the phrase in the relevant sense, but that is a relay, not Marcus’s own use; the quotation can supply an outside lead to Chollet’s dated text only.

Withdraw the proposed move to Solaiman: the phrase describes the GPT-2 Explorer interface, not the model-as-mere-autocomplete characterization. An interface affordance and that characterization are distinct senses, even though the interface uses a language model.

method.blind: All 178 Part A assignments were committed at 7d8c133e52019ccf68296aae1243ec0da8df91cf before either prelaunch audit file was opened. Only PA-01, PA-02 and PA-58 findings were read for Part B. Four later corrections retain their blindDecision and are labeled post-blind.
method.search: Search every stored source title and evidence passage across all collections, with claims and entity descriptions as discovery aids. Inspect candidate passages and full source text where accessible. Titles count for terms. Separate an author’s own wording from quotations or forwarded material. Compare attestation dates; retain claimed and publication dates separately.
method.limits: The JSON dataset stores selected passages and bibliographic descriptions, not the complete bodies of all 2007 sources. A global search of those stored fields is not a full-text re-read of every linked publication. Entries specify original retrievals and unresolved source-body or date issues. Negative search results do not establish absence.
method.external: Outside texts are leads only. No dataset or application files are changed.
method.headlineScope: Maintainer clarified during Part A: preserve headline stance, author and tier scope while searching all collections. An earlier articulation is not substituted for a contesting headline; another author is not substituted in the author-bounded collection.
method.senseRule: Maintainer clarification of 2026-11-02: a term candidate must use the name in the proposition's sense. A literal occurrence with a different referent receives different sense, not move. Naming need not endorse or fully articulate the proposition. Date, register, author and tier constraints remain separate.
method.nameUnit: A term headline covers the proposition’s listed alternative names in the same sense. Part B exposed four blind decisions that had ranked the selected spelling too narrowly; their corrections are explicit.

results.proposition: Intelligence explosion
results.criterion: A machine (or machine-augmented) intelligence, once capable enough, increases intelligence further through its own design or research capacity, giving a runaway or rapidly compounding rise.
results.name: intelligence explosion
results.claimText: Good’s chapter argues that an ultraintelligent machine, surpassing people at every intellectual activity including the design of machines, could design still better machines, so that there would be an "intelligence explosion" leaving human intelligence far behind.

claimDate.note: Year of Advances in Computers, volume 6, as catalogued by Open Library; the current Crossref record gives 1966. The discrepancy is unresolved.

claimed.note: The chapter’s footnote on p. 31 names talks in October 1962 and January 1963, a first draft of April 1963 and a slightly emended version of May 1964. None was retrieved, so the wording is not dated to them.

results.qualification: The chapter gives no timescale and says nothing about concealment. For the explosion it cites its references [22], [34] and [44]: Good’s 1951 review of a book by D. R. Hartree, an IBM report of 1959 (RC-115) and "The social implications of artificial intelligence" in The Scientist Speculates (1963); none was retrieved. An Internet Archive full-text search for the phrase in items indexed before 1965 found only unresolved or misdated hits.

evidence.passage: A machine that surpasses every intellectual activity of any person would also surpass people at designing machines; it could therefore design even better machines, and there would then be an "intelligence explosion", leaving human intelligence far behind.

results.proposition: Fast or hard takeoff
results.criterion: The transition from roughly human-level to far superhuman capability happens over a short period (hours to months), or is named as a “hard” or “fast” takeoff, as opposed to a gradual transition over years or decades. A transition described only as rapid, or rapid relative to biological or historical change, without such a period, does not meet the criterion.

results.proposition: Recursive self-improvement

results.proposition: Deceptive alignment
results.criterion: A trained or learned system that is not aligned behaves as if aligned during training because doing so serves another objective, for example to avoid modification and act on that objective later.
results.name: deceptive alignment
results.claimText: The introduction to Risks from Learned Optimization, posted 2019-05-31, says a sufficiently capable misaligned mesa-optimiser could learn to behave as if it were aligned without being robustly aligned, and names this situation deceptive alignment.

claimDate.note: Posting time 2019-05-31T23:44:53Z, under the account evhub; the post itself names all five authors. The first stored revision is timestamped 2019-05-31T01:05:35Z, before posting: a draft time, not public use.

results.qualification: The earliest located use of the term, five days before the part devoted to it (2019-06-05), which states the mechanism, and before arXiv v1; it is not evidence of coinage.

evidence.passage: a sufficiently capable misaligned mesa-optimizer could learn to behave as if it were aligned without actually being robustly aligned. We will call this situation deceptive alignment.

results.proposition: Orthogonality of intelligence and goals
results.criterion: An AI system's level of intelligence and its final goals can vary independently: a highly intelligent system could pursue more or less any final goal, so high intelligence does not by itself bring goals that are benevolent or compatible with human interests.
results.name: orthogonality thesis
results.claimText: Bostrom's paper of 2012 states the orthogonality thesis: that intelligence and final goals are orthogonal axes along which possible agents can freely vary, so that more or less any level of intelligence could in principle be combined with more or less any final goal.

claimDate.note: Date of publication, as the source gives it.

results.qualification: Earliest located use of the name “orthogonality thesis” among the texts the searches found; it is not evidence of coinage. The paper states the thesis 'with some caveats' and holds that it concerns logical possibility, not that arbitrary goals would be easy to instil.

evidence.locator: Section 1.2, The orthogonality thesis, PDF p. 3
evidence.passage: Intelligence and final goals are orthogonal axes along which possible agents can freely vary. In other words, more or less any level of intelligence could in principle be combined with more or less any final goal.

The orthogonality thesis suggests that we cannot blithely assume that a superintelligence will necessarily share any of the final values stereotypically associated with wisdom and intellectual development in humans

results.proposition: Instrumental convergence
results.criterion: Agents with a wide range of final goals would tend to pursue the same intermediate goals, such as self-preservation, keeping their goals unchanged, acquiring resources or power, or improving themselves, because these serve almost any final goal.
results.name: convergent instrumental
results.claimText: Bostrom's paper of 2012 states the instrumental convergence thesis: that several instrumental values would raise the chances of an agent's goal being realised for a wide range of final goals and situations, and so are likely to be pursued by many intelligent agents.

claimDate.note: Date of publication, as the source gives it.

results.qualification: A statement of the author's argument, not evidence that it holds for actual systems. The paper adds that the thesis predicts which instrumental values would be pursued, not the specific actions taken. Not evidence of coinage of the term.

evidence.passage: Several instrumental values can be identified which are convergent in the sense that their attainment would increase the chances of the agent’s goal being realized for a wide range of final goals and a wide range of situations

An agent with such a final goal would have a convergent instrumental reason, in many situations, to acquire an unlimited amount of physical resources and, if possible, to eliminate potential threats to itself and its goal system.

results.proposition: Inner or deceptive misalignment
results.criterion: A system produced by training or search can come to pursue an objective other than the one its training specified (the training signal or loss), while performing well on that training objective; an objective that is only misspecified by its developers does not meet the criterion; this includes, but is not limited to, a system that behaves as aligned during training or evaluation in order to pursue another objective later.
results.name: goal misgeneralization
results.claimText: Shah, Varma, Kumar, Phuong, Krakovna, Uesato and Kenton's paper of October 2022 states that a learned system may competently pursue an undesired goal that gives good performance in training, even when the specification is correct, and calls this goal misgeneralization.

claimDate.note: Date of the arXiv v1 submission.

results.qualification: Records the paper's definition, its examples in current deep-learning systems and its hypotheticals about more capable systems; the authors describe the hypotheticals as speculative and state that how likely the failure is in practice needs further work.

evidence.passage: an AI system may pursue an undesired goal even when the specification is correct, in the case of goal misgeneralization
the learned program competently pursues an undesired goal that leads to good performance in training situations but bad performance in novel test situations
we would also like to see additional work investigating how likely goal misgeneralization is in practice

results.proposition: Difficulty of alignment
results.criterion: Making an advanced AI system reliably pursue the goals its developers intend (aligning it) is a hard, unsolved technical problem that will not be solved by default in the ordinary course of development.
results.name: alignment problem
results.claimText: Russell's comment in the 2019 thread states that machines are already built on the assumption of a fixed, known objective, that this becomes more untenable as they become more powerful, and that there is no hope of solving value alignment by specifying the right value function offline.

claimDate.note: Dated by the LessWrong copy of 4 October 2019. The Facebook thread follows the Scientific American piece of 26 September 2019; the copy gives no date for individual comments.

attested.note: The wording is known from the LessWrong copy, whose compiler states that he improved formatting and fixed typos; the Facebook original was not compared.

results.qualification: States the difficulty for the standard model of AI and argues for changing it; not a claim that alignment cannot be achieved in any way. Each comment is the participant's own words in a relayed copy; the record states what the comment says in this thread, not the author's view at another date.

evidence.locator: Comment Thread #2, Stuart Russell (reply to Francesca Rossi)
evidence.passage: There is no hope of "solving the value alignment problem" in the sense of figuring out the right value function offline and putting it into the machine. We need to change the way we do AI.

results.proposition: Control or purpose specification
results.criterion: A claim that people may be unable to keep the ability to direct, correct or stop capable machines (the control half), or that a machine may pursue the purpose as specified rather than the purpose intended (the specification half). Loss of the power to stop machines through dependence counts for the control half; a bare prediction that machines will be superior does not.
results.claimText: The 1863 letter "Darwin among the Machines" argues that if destroying every machine is impossible, people have already raised a race of machines they cannot destroy and are acquiescent in their bondage.

claimDate.note: Issue date of The Press, vol. III, issue 192, p. 1, in the Papers Past record.

results.qualification: The control half of the proposition, reached through dependence: the argument is conditional, and the letter gives machines no aims, no concealment and no self-improvement. The pseudonymous letter uses satirical devices, such as presenting its subject "gratis to the members of the Philosophical Society" and an appended note on rudimentary organs in machines, and in 1901 Butler named it as the first part of Erewhon written (read in a Project Gutenberg transcription that names no source printing; no 1901 printing was compared); whether it is earnest is uncertain.

evidence.locator: Penultimate paragraph, beginning "Our opinion is that war to the death", after the call to destroy every machine; column-image segment 5 of 6
evidence.passage: this at once proves that the mischief is already done, that our servitude has commenced in good earnest, that we have raised a race of beings whom it is beyond our power to destroy, and that we are not only enslaved but are absolutely acquiescent in our bondage.

evidence.locator: Preface to the Revised Edition (dated 1901-08-07), second paragraph
evidence.passage: The first part of “Erewhon” written was an article headed “Darwin among the Machines,” and signed Cellarius.

results.proposition: Intelligence explosion
results.criterion: A machine (or machine-augmented) intelligence, once capable enough, increases intelligence further through its own design or research capacity, giving a runaway or rapidly compounding rise.
results.claimText: Good’s chapter argues that an ultraintelligent machine, surpassing people at every intellectual activity including the design of machines, could design still better machines, so that there would be an "intelligence explosion" leaving human intelligence far behind.

claimDate.note: Year of Advances in Computers, volume 6, as catalogued by Open Library; the current Crossref record gives 1966. The discrepancy is unresolved.

claimed.note: The chapter’s footnote on p. 31 names talks in October 1962 and January 1963, a first draft of April 1963 and a slightly emended version of May 1964. None was retrieved, so the wording is not dated to them.

results.qualification: The chapter gives no timescale and says nothing about concealment. For the explosion it cites its references [22], [34] and [44]: Good’s 1951 review of a book by D. R. Hartree, an IBM report of 1959 (RC-115) and "The social implications of artificial intelligence" in The Scientist Speculates (1963); none was retrieved. An Internet Archive full-text search for the phrase in items indexed before 1965 found only unresolved or misdated hits.

evidence.locator: Section 2, "Ultraintelligent Machines and Their Value", printed p. 33 (scan page 3)
evidence.passage: A machine that surpasses every intellectual activity of any person would also surpass people at designing machines; it could therefore design even better machines, and there would then be an "intelligence explosion", leaving human intelligence far behind.

results.proposition: Switching it off if it becomes dangerous
results.criterion: An explicit claim that an advanced AI system that became dangerous could simply be switched off or corrected, on the premise that a capable goal-directed system would not act against its own shutdown or modification, so that a shutdown or correction mechanism can be added to it, or that people would recognise in time when it had become dangerous enough to use one.
results.claimText: The Extropians message “Re: Trans- vs. Non-human” (1996-12-08) contests Y01. Replying to Steve Witham, who asked why certain values should not be 'inerasably etched' on a newborn Power, he argues that a Power would work against limits imposed on it, turning the constraint into a contest inside the Power's own mind that the Power would almost certainly win.

claimDate.note: Archive author index lists the message as "Sun, 08 Dec 1996 22:39:23 -0600" under "Eliezer Yudkowsky".

results.qualification: Premise addressed: A capable goal-directed system will not act to prevent its own shutdown or modification, and a shutdown or correction mechanism can simply be added to it. The argument rests on his 1996 view that an unconstrained Power would be ethical (see his Extropians messages of 1996-11-22); his conclusion at the time was to leave Powers unconstrained. results.criterion: An explicit claim that a sufficiently intelligent system will work out ethics and act well, on the premise that greater intelligence by itself brings benevolent goals, or that a sufficiently intelligent mind would discover a true or universally compelling morality and be bound to act on it.
results.claimText: The Extropians message “Re: IA vs. AI was: longevity vs singularity” (1999-08-01) contests Y02. In a long reply to den Otter, he points to his old Extropians posts and the old version of 'Staring Into the Singularity' as showing how he moved from assuming superintelligences would be good and nice to humans to not knowing what absolute good is.

claimDate.note: Archive author index lists the message as "1999-08-01" under "Eliezer S. Yudkowsky".

results.qualification: Premise addressed: Greater intelligence by itself brings benevolent goals. Retrospective; refers back to his 1996 posts (his Extropians messages of 1996-11-22) and 'Staring Into the Singularity'. Rejects the assurance of benevolence (the premise that greater intelligence by itself brings benevolent goals) only. The quoted sentence continues 'but if there is one I suppose the Singularity is the best way to serve it', and the same message says 'any garden-variety superintelligence should be able to handle' figuring out the meaning of life, so he did not yet reject the premise that a sufficiently intelligent mind would discover a true morality and be bound to act on it; that came in late 2000 (his SL4 message of 2000-11-13). Two days later (his Extropians message of 1999-08-03) he wrote: 'When I thought AIs would be benevolent, I said so. When I realized I didn't have the vaguest notion, I said so.' The quotation ends before he adds that if there is a meaning of life, the Singularity is the best way to serve it. The quoted words reject the first premise only; the unquoted continuation keeps a conditional form of the second, rejected later (his SL4 message of 2000-11-13 and his 2008 post ‘That Tiny Note of Discord’).

results.proposition: Essential unautomated tasks bottleneck growth
results.criterion: The text states that growth is constrained because essential tasks or inputs remain unautomated or unimproved, or are automated only slowly, so that automating many but not all tasks, or automating them gradually, does not by itself produce explosive growth (Baumol's cost disease; an elasticity of substitution below one between tasks or between information and other inputs). Reasons why automation stays incomplete or slow (technical difficulty, physical-world tasks, training data, regulation of AI training or deployment, slow adoption) belong here.
results.claimText: Nordhaus, “Are We Approaching an Economic Singularity? Information Technology and the Future of Economic Growth” (2015-09) articulates G04. Rapid improvement in information technology raises aggregate growth only if information substitutes well for other inputs in production, or for other goods in consumption. The inelastic case of the same model: growth converges to that of the slowest input.

results.proposition: AI as a general-purpose technology with lagging productivity
results.criterion: A text that calls AI a general-purpose technology and states that measured productivity gains lag adoption because of complementary investment (for example a J-curve or a productivity paradox).
results.claimText: Brynjolfsson, Rock, Syverson, “Artificial Intelligence and the Modern Productivity Paradox: A Clash of Expectations and Statistics” (2017-11) articulates M03. Argues that implementation lags, rather than false hopes, mismeasurement or redistribution, are the likeliest main explanation of the gap between AI expectations and slowing measured productivity. Concludes that AI breakthroughs have not yet diffused and their complementary changes depress measured productivity at first; the same conclusion calls AI the core of "a new, economically important potential GPT".

results.proposition: AI’s productivity effect over the next decade
results.criterion: A text that gives a stated estimate of AI's effect on aggregate productivity or GDP over a horizon of about ten years from the text's date. The figure and horizon are recorded; the proposition is neutral as to size.
results.claimText: Acemoglu, “The Simple Macroeconomics of AI” (2024-04-05) articulates M08. Acemoglu applies a Hulten's-theorem task framework to exposure and cost-saving estimates to bound AI's ten-year TFP effect, against much larger forecasts (Goldman Sachs, McKinsey). Allowing for hard-to-learn tasks where AI gains are smaller lowers the ten-year TFP bound. Acemoglu converts the TFP bounds to GDP effects under two investment-response assumptions. The author-hosted version of 5 April 2024 gives no more than 0.71% over ten years, and less than 0.55% allowing for hard tasks; the NBER version of May 2024 gives 0.66% and 0.53%.

claimDate.note: Title page of the author-hosted version: "April 5, 2024". The NBER version (cover "May 2024") gives different figures; its passages are dated May 2024 by their source.

(Second passage) The same abstract’s figure after allowing for hard-to-learn tasks. (Third passage) NBER version of May 2024. Material quantitative claim: an upper bound on total (not annual) US TFP gain over 10 years from May 2024; illustrative back-of-the-envelope calculation resting on Eloundou et al. (2023) exposure, Svanberg et al. (2024) feasibility and experimental cost-saving estimates. Needs targeted recheck. This is total-factor productivity, not GDP, over ten years in total; the paper also reports an alternative of about 0.89%. The later journal version was not compared. (Fourth passage) Material quantitative claim: upper bound on total 10-year TFP gain, using 'speculative' assumptions (at most 73% easy tasks; hard-task gains about one quarter of easy). Needs targeted recheck. The figure is total TFP over ten years. (Fifth passage) Material quantitative claim: 10-year total GDP effects conditional on investment response; Acemoglu notes extra investment-driven GDP does not add to welfare. The introduction gives a lower hard-task GDP bound of 0.90%. Needs targeted recheck.

results.reason: The cited blog conclusion names high-bandwidth ground communications as an engineering challenge, but does not explicitly state which orbital-compute workloads are excluded or limited, as the criterion requires. results.proposition: No practical repair of hardware in orbit
results.criterion: Failed hardware in orbit cannot practically be repaired or replaced by technicians as on Earth, so failures must be met by redundancy, module replacement or launches.
results.claimText: ESPI Report 98 (November 2025) states that in-orbit servicing remains so costly that deorbiting a failed satellite and launching a replacement is generally considered more cost-effective than sending crews for repairs, and that the maintenance cycle of a space-based data centre is expected to depend heavily on redundancy, which itself increases costs.

claimDate.note: Date of publication on the European Space Policy Institute’s report page; the PDF prints “Published: November 2025”.

results.qualification: Earliest located among the texts found by the pack’s searches of 2026-10-28 and the cross-family check’s bounded search of 2026-10-29/30; not a claim that no earlier text exists. A self-funded policy study; it also reports experts’ suggestion of replacing servers on a five-year cycle by hot-swapping modules, and the development of autonomous repair systems. It replaces the Suncatcher paper (22 November 2025) as earliest located, a correction recorded on the collection page.

evidence.passage: The cost of in-orbit servicing remains extremely high, to the extent that deorbiting a failed satellite and launching a replacement is generally considered more cost-effective than sending robotic or human crews for repairs

results.proposition: Orbital compute costs more than compute on Earth
results.criterion: At current or assumed launch and spacecraft prices, computing in orbit costs more than equivalent computing on Earth.
results.claimText: ESPI Report 98 (November 2025) models gigawatt-scale space-based data centres against a terrestrial benchmark and finds that, under its modelling assumptions, a constellation architecture has double the benchmark’s capital cost and more than triple its operating cost, and a monolithic architecture an operating cost 38% higher.

claimDate.note: Date of publication on the European Space Policy Institute’s report page; the PDF prints “Published: November 2025”.

results.qualification: Earliest located among the texts found by the pack’s searches of 2026-10-28 and the cross-family check’s bounded search of 2026-10-29/30; not a claim that no earlier text exists. Architecture-specific and conditional: the report finds the monolithic architecture’s capital cost comparable to the benchmark’s and, with IT hardware lasting over three years, cheaper over its lifetime, and it concludes that the potential for economic feasibility is high if component lifespan and cost, robotic maintenance and launch prices improve. Not a finding for all orbital compute. It replaces Turyshev’s preprint (April 2026) as earliest located, a correction recorded on the collection page.

evidence.locator: PDF p. 46 (printed p. 42), Annex A, “Results and Discussion”
evidence.passage: the constellation architecture is not nearly as competitive as the monolithic architecture in the GW-scale. Its CapEx is double the TBDCs and its OpEx more than triple.

evidence.locator: PDF p. 46 (printed p. 42), Annex A, “Results and Discussion”
evidence.passage: With respect to OpEx it’s still 38% more expensive than the TBDC given the modelling assumptions.
In conclusion, the potential for SBDCs being economically feasible is high.

The report says the monolithic architecture becomes cheaper than the benchmark over its lifetime if IT hardware lasts over three years, uses a two-year lifetime in its model, names a launch cost under $150/kg among its conditions for viability, and gives expected costs without a measure of uncertainty.

results.criterion: The text states that AI systems already deployed or publicly available at the time of writing increase the ability of an actor seeking to cause biological harm, relative to the resources otherwise available to that actor.
results.claimText: RAND's report on the operational risks of AI in large-scale biological attacks (RR-A2977-2, 25 January 2024) states that it found no statistically significant difference in the overall viability of biological weapon attack plans generated with or without the aid of the large language models it tested, and that such planning is beyond the capability frontier of the models available in summer 2023.

claimDate.note: Publication date given on the RAND landing page for RR-A2977-2.

results.qualification: The record documents what this report states, with the report's own scope: the two models it tested, as available in summer 2023, and the viability of written plans as its measure. The report states that it does not quantify how far beyond the frontier the task lies. The record is not evidence that the proposition is false, does not generalise to other models or later dates, and implies no influence between texts. Earliest located contesting text among those searched in this pass; not a claim that no earlier one exists. The report is the dataset document the evaluations records also cite: both strands of the pack retrieved the same file, and the admission keeps one document and one source for it. The report's body discusses specific agents and delivery considerations. Only its conclusions passages are cited; that content was excluded and is not paraphrased.

evidence.passage: With respect to overall viability, we found no statistically significant difference between the biological weapon attack plans generated with or without the aid of LLMs.
Our findings indicate that biological weapon attack planning is beyond the capability frontier of LLMs available in summer 2023.

In this report, we do not quantify the extent to which biological weapon attack planning lies beyond the existing capability frontier of LLMs, only that it does. The durability of this finding in relation to future developments in LLM technology is therefore an open question.
